questions.question: LSI, VLSI & ULSI chips were used in which generation?
questions.explanation: LSI, VLSI and ULSI chips pack thousands to millions of components on one chip, and they belong to the fourth generation, which produced the microprocessor. The third generation (C) used smaller-scale integrated circuits (SSI and MSI), while the first and second generations used vacuum tubes and transistors.

questions.question: When was the transistor invented?
questions.explanation: The transistor was invented in 1947 by William Shockley and his colleagues at Bell Labs, and it later replaced vacuum tubes in second-generation computers. 1938 (option B) is too early, while by 1958 (option C) transistors were already being used in computers. 1968 (option D) is in the integrated circuit era.

questions.question: Most important advantage of an IC is its

options.a: Easy replacement in case of circuit failure

questions.explanation: An integrated circuit puts many components on one chip with very few soldered joints, so it is extremely reliable, and that is its most important advantage. Lower cost (C) and lower power use (D) are real benefits too, but the big step forward was reliability. ICs are not easy to repair (A); a faulty chip is replaced as a whole.

questions.question: UNIVAC was a first generation computer. What is its full form?
questions.explanation: UNIVAC stands for Universal Automatic Computer, and it was the first commercial computer, delivered to the US Census Bureau in 1951. The other options change Universal or Automatic into words that are not part of the name.

questions.question: The Napier's bone was invented in what year?
questions.explanation: John Napier described his calculating rods, Napier's bones, in 1617, the year his book on them was published. 1642 (A) is when Pascal built his calculator, 1801 (D) is linked to the Jacquard loom, and 1716 and 1622 do not match Napier's invention.

questions.question: Below are characteristics of first generations of computers except ______
questions.explanation: First generation computers were very expensive to maintain because their vacuum tubes burned out often and they needed lots of power and cooling, so cheap maintenance is the false statement. Needing experts (A), being too costly for individuals (B), taking huge space (C) and producing heat (E) are all true of that generation.

questions.question: What is the full meaning of the acronym ENIAC?
questions.explanation: ENIAC stands for Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer, one of the earliest first-generation electronic computers. Each of the other options changes a word, for example 'integration' instead of 'integrator' (A), 'Electric' instead of 'Electronic' (C), or 'numeric' instead of 'numerical' (E), so they are not the correct name.

questions.question: What was the processor speed of the third generation of computers?
questions.explanation: Third generation processors worked in nanoseconds, meaning one billionth of a second. One millionth of a second (D) is a microsecond, the speed of the second generation, and 256Mb/s and 1024M/s (C, E) are data rates, not processing times.

questions.question: _______ is credited with developing the punch card
questions.explanation: Herman Hollerith developed punched cards for processing data and built tabulating machines that used them for the 1890 US census. Option E, the Jacquard loom, is a machine rather than a person, though it did use punched cards earlier to control weaving patterns. Blaise Pascal (C) built a mechanical calculator, and Ada Lovelace (D) is known for writing early programs.

questions.question: The analytical engine was powered by ________
questions.explanation: Charles Babbage designed the Analytical Engine as a mechanical machine to be driven by a steam engine, the main power source of his time. Electrical power (A and B), solar power (D) and batteries (E) were not what it was designed to run on.

questions.question: The processors on which the fourth generation of computers were built is _____
questions.explanation: Fourth generation computers were built on microprocessors, where a whole CPU sits on a single chip made with VLSI. Transistors (B) belong to the second generation, and thermionic (vacuum) valves (E) to the first.

questions.question: Which among the following generation computer had expensive operation cost ?
questions.explanation: First generation computers were the most expensive to run because their vacuum tubes used large amounts of electricity, produced great heat that needed cooling, and burned out often. Each later generation (B, D, E, A) became cheaper and more efficient to operate.

questions.question: The first generation of computers used:
questions.explanation: First generation computers used vacuum tubes for their circuits and memory, which made them huge and hot. Transistors (A) came in the second generation, integrated circuits (C) in the third, and microprocessors (D) in the fourth.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of second-generation computers?
questions.explanation: Second generation computers replaced vacuum tubes with transistors, making them smaller, faster and more reliable. Vacuum tubes (A) belong to the first generation, microchips (C) to later generations, and AI (D) to the fifth.

questions.question: The ENIAC computer belongs to which generation?
questions.explanation: ENIAC was a first generation computer built with thousands of vacuum tubes. The second, third and fourth generations (B, C, D) used transistors, integrated circuits and microprocessors, all of which came after ENIAC.

questions.question: The invention of the microprocessor marked the beginning of which generation?
questions.explanation: The microprocessor, a whole CPU on one chip, began the fourth generation and made microcomputers possible. The second generation (A) used transistors, the third (B) used integrated circuits, and the fifth (D) focuses on artificial intelligence.

questions.question: Which of the following was a limitation of first-generation computers?
questions.explanation: First generation computers produced a lot of heat because of their vacuum tubes, and that was one of their main problems. They were not compact (A), fast (C) or low on energy use (D); they were huge, slow by today's standards and used a lot of power.

questions.question: In which generation of computers were high-level programming languages such as FORTRAN and COBOL first developed?
questions.explanation: High-level languages such as FORTRAN and COBOL were invented and first used during the second generation, alongside assembly language, on transistor-based computers. The third generation (option C) brought more high-level languages, but it did not start them. First-generation machines (option A) were programmed in machine language, and the fourth generation (option D) came much later.

questions.question: Which generation of computers introduced the use of integrated circuits?
questions.explanation: The third generation introduced integrated circuits, which put many transistors on one silicon chip. The first generation (A) used vacuum tubes, the second (B) used separate transistors, and the fourth (D) used microprocessors built with very large scale integration.

questions.question: The abacus is considered a precursor to modern computers because it:
questions.explanation: The abacus is seen as an early ancestor of the computer because it helped people do arithmetic quickly. It used no electricity (A), stored nothing digitally (C) and had no network (D); it was just beads on rods.

questions.question: The transition from vacuum tubes to transistors resulted in:
questions.explanation: Replacing vacuum tubes with transistors made computers smaller, faster and more reliable, and they used less power. Options A, B and D describe the opposite of what happened.

questions.question: Who is considered the "father of the computer"?
questions.explanation: Charles Babbage is called the father of the computer because he designed the Difference Engine and the Analytical Engine, which had the main parts of a modern computer. Alan Turing (B) is known for the theory of computation, and Bill Gates (C) and Steve Jobs (D) are known for software and personal computers.

questions.question: The first true adding machine was invented in 1642 by ____.
questions.explanation: Blaise Pascal, a French mathematician, built the Pascaline in 1642, a mechanical calculator that could add and subtract and is often called the first true adding machine. Charles Babbage (option D) designed the Difference and Analytical Engines much later, in the 1800s. Options A, B and C are misspellings or made-up names, not real inventors.

questions.question: A German philosopher, Gottfried Leibnitz, invented the calculator in ____.
questions.explanation: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, a German philosopher and mathematician, designed his calculating machine (the Stepped Reckoner) in 1671. It improved on Pascal's design by also multiplying and dividing. The other dates are wrong: 1571 is long before such machines, and 1867, 1909 and 1911 are far too late.

questions.question: EDVAC stands for ____.
questions.explanation: EDVAC stands for Electronic Discrete Variable Automatic Computer, one of the early first-generation stored-program computers. Option E is the only choice with the correct key words 'Electronic Discrete Variable'. 'Dual Value' and 'Discrete Value' (options B, C and D) are wrong, and EDVAC was electronic, not 'elaborate' (options A and B).

questions.question: The Analytic and Difference engines were invented by ____.
questions.explanation: Charles Babbage, an English mathematician, designed the Difference Engine and the Analytical Engine in the 1800s. That is why he is called the father of the computer. Blaise Pascal (option E) built an adding machine in 1642, and options A, B and C are misspellings or made-up names.

questions.question: Which of these scientists worked on the ENIAC project?

options.a: John Von Neumann, Steve Jobs, Aristotle
options.b: Bill Gates, Steve Jobs, Herman Goldstine
options.c: John Von Neumann, Herman Goldstine, Arthur W. Burks
options.d: Herman Goldstine, Steve Jobs, Arthur W. Burks
options.e: John Von Neumann, Bill Gates, Herman Goldstine

questions.explanation: John von Neumann, Herman Goldstine and Arthur W. Burks were all linked to the ENIAC project in the 1940s, and later to the design of the EDVAC that followed it. Steve Jobs and Bill Gates (in options A, B, D and E) were born long after ENIAC was built. Aristotle was an ancient Greek philosopher.

questions.question: Which of these characterize first generation computers?

options.a: They are portable and easy to use
options.b: They occupy large space and require perpetual human intervention
options.c: They occupy large space and have high processing capability
options.d: They dissipate a lot heat and have small circuits with no human intervention
options.e: They were easily programmable and dissipate little heat.

questions.explanation: First-generation computers were huge machines built from vacuum tubes and filled whole rooms. They had no operating system, so human operators had to set switches and handle punched cards. Option C is wrong because their processing capability was low by later standards, and options A, D and E describe later generations: portable, cool-running and easy to program.

questions.question: An example of first generation computer is ____.
questions.explanation: The UNIVAC 1103 was a vacuum-tube machine from the early 1950s, part of the UNIVAC family of first-generation computers. The Compaq Presario (option A) was a personal computer from the 1990s, and UNIX servers (option B) are modern machines. 'IBM1021' (option C) is not a known first-generation model.

questions.question: First generation computers used ____.
questions.explanation: First-generation computers were built with thermionic valves (vacuum tubes) connected by wires; the second generation replaced these with transistors and diodes. Transistors (options A and E) belong to the second generation, and integrated circuits to the third. Printed circuit boards (option D) came later as well.

questions.question: The first generation of computers began in the ____.
questions.explanation: The first generation of electronic computers began in the mid-1940s, with vacuum-tube machines such as ENIAC completed around 1946. The mid-1930s (option B) came before any electronic digital computer was in use. The mid-1960s, 1970s and 1980s (options C, D and E) belong to the later integrated-circuit and microprocessor generations.

questions.question: Integrated circuits were first used in ____ computers.
questions.explanation: Integrated circuits (ICs), which put many transistors on one small silicon chip, were the main technology of the third generation (around the mid-1960s). First-generation computers used vacuum tubes and second-generation computers used individual transistors (options A and B). The fourth generation moved on to microprocessors.

questions.question: In third generation computers, MOS stands for ____.
questions.explanation: MOS stands for Metal Oxide Semiconductor, the transistor technology used to build integrated circuits from the third generation onward. It has nothing to do with operating systems, so options A, C and E are wrong. Option B, 'Medium Ordered Systems', is not a real term.

questions.question: The introduction of microprocessors led to the production of ____ micro-computers.
questions.explanation: A microprocessor is a whole CPU on a single chip, and it made small, affordable microcomputers possible in the fourth generation (1970s onward). The third generation (option D) used integrated circuits but not complete CPUs on one chip. There is no officially recognised sixth generation (option B).

questions.question: The early form of computer memory which was made up of tiny rings of magnetic materials, threaded on wires by hand is called ____.
questions.explanation: Magnetic core memory, usually just called 'cores', was made of tiny rings of magnetic material threaded onto wires by hand. Each ring stored one bit. Semiconductor memory (option C) replaced cores later, and options A, B and E are not real names for this technology.

questions.question: Fourth generation computer were built on
questions.explanation: Fourth-generation computers were built on microprocessor technology, made possible by very large scale integration (VLSI), which puts a whole CPU on one chip. Vacuum tubes (option C) belong to the first generation, transistors (option A) to the second, and simple integrated circuits (option D) to the third.

questions.question: The inventor of the difference engine was
questions.explanation: Charles Babbage, an English mathematician, designed the Difference Engine in the 1820s to calculate mathematical tables automatically. Gottfried Leibniz (option C) built a calculating machine in the 1600s, and Samuel Morland (option D) also made early mechanical calculators. John von Neumann (option B) is known for the stored-program computer design of the 1940s.

questions.question: The following features make the Analytical Engine different from the Difference Engine except?

options.a: It is to be powered by a steam engine
options.b: It is similar to difference engine in design.
options.c: The arithmetic logic unit will be able to perform all the four arithmetic operation
options.d: The output requires a printer, curve plotter and a bell

questions.explanation: Being similar to the Difference Engine in design is not something that makes the Analytical Engine different, so B is the exception. The Analytical Engine was planned to run on steam power, to have a "mill" able to do all four arithmetic operations, and to produce output through a printer, curve plotter and bell. A, C and D are therefore genuine differences.

questions.question: Who invented the first adding machine?
questions.explanation: Blaise Pascal built the Pascaline in the 1640s, which is widely regarded as the first mechanical adding machine. Charles Babbage (C) came much later with the Difference and Analytical Engines, and Leibniz (E) built a calculator that improved on Pascal's design.

questions.question: How were data to be inputed on the adding machine done and results displayed?

options.c: They were entered on dials and results were read from dial positions

questions.explanation: Pascal's adding machine was fully mechanical: numbers were entered by turning dials, and results were read from the positions of the dials. Keyboards, mice, touch pens and scanners (A, B, D, E) are modern electronic devices that did not exist then.

questions.question: Who designed the first automatic calculating machine different from the calculator?
questions.explanation: Charles Babbage designed the Difference Engine and then the Analytical Engine, automatic calculating machines that went far beyond a simple calculator. Blaise Pascal built a mechanical adding machine, which is a calculator, while Alan Turing and Von Neumann worked much later, in the 20th century.

questions.question: The concept of storing within the machine itself, alterable instructions that directs the operation of a computer is called
questions.explanation: The stored program concept means the instructions are kept inside the computer's own memory, just like data, so they can be changed and run automatically. Programming (A) is the act of writing instructions, while Pascal and BASIC (B and C) are programming languages.

questions.question: The concept that differentiate the computer from all other data processing device was introduced by a mathematician named
questions.explanation: The stored program concept, which separates a true computer from other data processing devices, was put forward by the mathematician John von Neumann. Charles Babbage (B) designed the Analytical Engine, which used punched cards for its instructions instead of storing a program in memory, and Pascal (A) built a mechanical adding machine.

questions.question: The first mechanical computing aid was
questions.explanation: The abacus, a frame of beads that slide on rods, is the earliest known mechanical aid for counting and calculating. Sticks, fingers and stones (B, C, D) were used for counting, but they are not mechanical devices.

questions.question: What power source was used by the analytical engine?
questions.explanation: Charles Babbage designed the Analytical Engine to be driven by a steam engine, which was the main power source of his time. Electricity (B) was not used to power computing machines until much later.

questions.question: What was the input device for the analytical engine
questions.explanation: The Analytical Engine was to read its instructions and data from punched cards, an idea borrowed from the Jacquard loom. Scanners, keyboards, microphones and touch screens (A, B, D, E) are modern devices that did not exist in Babbage's time.

questions.question: What is the basic building block for the first generation of computers?
questions.explanation: First-generation computers such as ENIAC and UNIVAC used vacuum tubes as their basic electronic component for circuitry and memory. Transistors (B) replaced vacuum tubes in the second generation. Magnetic core (C) is a memory technology, and metallic semiconductor and solid-state parts (D, E) belong to later generations.

questions.question: The storage for the first generation of computers were
questions.explanation: First-generation computers stored data on magnetic drums and in delay-line memory. Flash drives, hard discs and optical discs (A, B and C) came much later, and valves (D) were the switching components, not the storage medium.

questions.question: The problems of the first generation of computers includes the following except?
questions.explanation: First-generation computers produced a lot of heat, used a lot of power, were expensive and needed engineers to install them. Large-scale integration (putting many components on one chip) was a later breakthrough, so it was not one of their problems.

questions.question: The circuitry of the second generation of computers were made up of
questions.explanation: In second-generation computers, the wires and vacuum valves of the first generation were replaced by printed circuits, diodes and transistors. Plain wires and cables (A and D) describe earlier machines, and address buses (C) are not a circuitry technology of a generation.

questions.question: What was the storage of the second generation of computers made of?
questions.explanation: Second-generation computers used magnetic core memory as their main storage, along with magnetic tape and disk for backing storage. Floppy disks and flash drives (A and B) arrived in later generations, and valves (E) were first-generation switching parts.

questions.question: What was the innovation behind third generation of computers
questions.explanation: Third-generation computers were built around the integrated circuit (IC), which put many transistors and other components on one small silicon chip. Diodes (A) were already used in the second generation, and the stored program idea (E) came earlier still.

questions.question: What is the full meaning of SSI?
questions.explanation: SSI stands for Small Scale Integration, the earliest level of chip technology, which places only a small number of components on one integrated circuit. The other options change "Scale" or "Integration" into wrong words.

questions.question: What is the full meaning of MSI?
questions.explanation: MSI stands for Medium Scale Integration, a step up from SSI, which places a moderate number of components (roughly tens to hundreds of gates) on one chip. Options A, C and D each replace one of the correct words.

questions.question: What is the full meaning of LSI?
questions.explanation: LSI stands for Large Scale Integration, chip technology that puts thousands of components on a single integrated circuit. The options with "sale", "Least" or "integrated" change one of the correct words.

questions.question: What was the memory made up of in the third generation of computers?
questions.explanation: Third-generation computers began using semiconductor memory such as DRAM and PROM, built as metal oxide semiconductor (MOS) chips in line with their integrated circuit technology. Vacuum tubes (B) and mercury delay lines (D) belong to the first generation, and punched cards (C) were an input medium, not memory.

questions.question: In what generation of computers did the design of operating systems begin?
questions.explanation: The third generation, built on integrated circuits, is when operating systems came into use, letting users work through keyboards and monitors instead of punched cards. First-generation machines (A) had no operating system, since human operators set switches by hand. The fourth generation (B) came later and brought microcomputer systems such as MS-DOS.

questions.question: ENIAC is an acronym for
questions.explanation: ENIAC stands for Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer, one of the earliest general-purpose electronic computers from the first generation. The other options change "Numerical", "Integrator" or "Computer" into similar but wrong words.

questions.question: Which of the combinations below was available during the first generation?

options.c: Magnetic core memory, Transistors, Mainframe computers.

questions.explanation: The first generation used mainframe computers built with valves (vacuum tubes) and memory drums for storage. Transistors (A, C and E) belong to the second generation, and minicomputers (D and E) came with the third generation.

questions.question: Printed circuits, diodes and transistors first appeared in the:
questions.explanation: Printed circuits, diodes and transistors replaced the wires and vacuum valves of the first generation, and they first appeared in second-generation computers. Integrated circuits, not discrete transistors, define the third generation (C).

questions.question: The Analytical engine was designed by ______
questions.explanation: Charles Babbage designed the Analytical Engine in the 1830s, a mechanical general-purpose computer with a mill (processor), a store (memory) and punched-card input. Joseph Jacquard (A) invented the punched-card loom that inspired it, and Herman Hollerith (B) built tabulating machines later.

questions.question: ______ is credited with introducing punched cards to data processing
questions.explanation: Herman Hollerith brought punched cards into data processing with his tabulating machine, which was used to process the 1890 US census. John Napier (C) is known for logarithms and Napier's bones, not punched cards, and Lady Lovelace (B) is remembered as the first programmer.

questions.question: Microcomputers are products of development in one of the following areas
questions.explanation: Microcomputers came out of the fourth generation, when very large scale integration (VLSI) made it possible to put a whole CPU on one chip, called the microprocessor. Option B mentions ICs and valves, which belong to earlier generations, while robotics in C has nothing to do with it.

questions.question: Use of binary numbers for storing data and the stored program concept were the ideas suggested by
questions.explanation: John von Neumann proposed storing both programs and data in memory as binary numbers, which is known as the stored-program concept. Eckert and Mauchly (E) built ENIAC, Hollerith (A) made punched-card tabulators, and the abacus (C) is a counting tool, not a person.

questions.question: Parallel processing is a highlight of
questions.explanation: Parallel processing, where many processors work on different parts of one program at the same time, is a key feature of fifth generation computers. Unix (A) is an operating system and the Intel 8080 (D) is a single early microprocessor, so neither is defined by parallel processing.

questions.question: The first programmable calculating device was developed by
questions.explanation: Charles Babbage designed the Analytical Engine, the first calculating machine meant to be programmed (using punched cards) to carry out different sequences of operations. Blaise Pascal's Pascaline (A) was an earlier mechanical calculator, but it could only add and subtract and could not be programmed.

questions.question: Integrated circuit was invented by Jack S. Kilby in ______
questions.explanation: Jack Kilby demonstrated the first integrated circuit in 1958, putting several electronic components on one small piece of semiconductor. 1948 (A) is around when the transistor appeared, and 1971 (D) is when the first commercial microprocessor came out.

questions.question: The DNA computer was successfully used in ____ by ____
questions.explanation: Leonard Adleman showed in 1994 that DNA molecules could be used to solve a computing problem, which is where DNA computing began. The other pairs refer to different milestones: Turing's abstract machine, Hollerith's tabulator and Pascal's calculator.

questions.question: The abstract machine was introduced in ____ by ____
questions.explanation: Alan Turing described his abstract computing machine, now called the Turing machine, in a paper published in 1936-37, and it laid the theoretical foundation of computer science. Pascal (A) built a mechanical calculator and Hollerith (B) built punched-card tabulators, which are physical machines, not abstract ones.

questions.question: Shor in ____ developed a quantum computing algorithm for solving a hard problem (factoring large numbers)
questions.explanation: Peter Shor published his quantum algorithm for factoring large numbers in 1994, showing that a quantum computer could in principle solve a problem that is extremely hard for ordinary computers. The years in A to D come well before this work.

questions.question: The difference between the technologies of the third and fourth generation computers was:

options.d: Improvement in scale of integration of ICs

questions.explanation: Both third and fourth generation computers used integrated circuits. The difference is that the fourth generation used much larger scales of integration (LSI and VLSI), which made the microprocessor possible. ICs alone (C) were already present in the third generation, and valves had already gone by then (A).

questions.question: The major component of the first generation computers was
questions.explanation: First generation computers were built with electronic valves (vacuum tubes), which made them huge, hot and unreliable. Transistors (B) came with the second generation, and large scale integration (C) came with the fourth.

questions.question: One of the following is not a feature of 3rd generation computers?
questions.explanation: Expert systems belong to the fifth generation, which focuses on artificial intelligence. ICs, medium-scale integration, procedural high-level languages and operating systems (B, C, D, E) are all features of the third generation.

questions.question: Second generation computers used this programming language
questions.explanation: Second generation computers are known for assembler (assembly language), which replaced raw machine code with short mnemonics. Machine language (E) is the mark of the first generation, while Pascal, Java and Ada (A, B, D) all came much later.

questions.question: The generation based on VLSI microprocessor
questions.explanation: Fourth-generation computers were built with very large scale integration (VLSI), which put a whole CPU on one chip, the microprocessor. The third generation (E) used smaller integrated circuits, and the fifth (B) is linked to artificial intelligence.

questions.question: The earliest mechanical aid to calculation was_______
questions.explanation: The abacus, a frame of beads on rods, was the earliest mechanical aid to calculation, and it is often called a bead frame. The other options (string wire, counting pearls, sticks, wooden bars) are not the name of this device.

questions.question: What does SSI stand for in transistor density in third generation of computers?
questions.explanation: SSI stands for Small Scale Integration, the earliest level of putting several transistors on one integrated circuit chip, used in third-generation computers. The other options change the wording (integrating, integrator, smaller) and are not the standard term.

questions.question: The third generation of computers were built on what technology?
questions.explanation: Third-generation computers were built with integrated circuits, which placed many transistors on one silicon chip. Transistors (A) belong to the second generation, vacuum tubes (C) to the first, and artificial intelligence (B) to the fifth.

questions.question: The analytical machine operated at what number base
questions.explanation: Babbage's Analytical Engine was a mechanical computer that stored and worked with numbers in decimal, base 10, using geared wheels with ten positions. Binary (E) only became standard later with electronic computers.

questions.question: Who invented ENIAC?
questions.explanation: ENIAC was built by J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly at the University of Pennsylvania. Charles Babbage (E) designed earlier mechanical engines, Pascal and Napier (B) made early calculating aids, and Hollerith (A) is known for punched-card machines.

questions.question: _____ generation of computer started with using vacuum tubes as the basic components.
questions.explanation: First-generation computers, such as ENIAC and UNIVAC, used vacuum tubes as their basic components. The second generation (D) replaced vacuum tubes with transistors, and the third (A) used integrated circuits.

questions.question: When was the first true adding machine invented?
questions.explanation: The first true adding machine was Blaise Pascal's Pascaline, built in 1642. The other years are just before or after this date.

questions.question: The standard astronomical and navigational table compilation was aided by what computing device?
questions.explanation: Charles Babbage designed the Difference Engine to calculate mathematical tables automatically, such as those used in astronomy and navigation, without human copying errors. The Analytical Engine (A) was his later general-purpose design, and the abacus (B) is a manual counting aid.

questions.question: What is the full meaning of the acronym EDVAC?
questions.explanation: EDVAC stands for Electronic Discrete Variable Automatic Computer, and option C gives all of these words correctly except Automatic. The other options change key words, such as Electrode, Varying, Value or Electric, so C is the best answer.

questions.question: An invention in the Bell Telephone laboratory that revolutionarise the whole of electronic engineering is called?
questions.explanation: The transistor, invented at Bell Telephone Laboratories in 1947, replaced the bulky vacuum tube and transformed electronics. Diodes and capacitors (B, C) already existed, and the chip (D) came later.

questions.question: Why was the circuitry of the second generation of computers referred to as 'solid state'

options.a: Because current flows through solid semiconductor material instead of a vacuum
options.d: Because electricity did not flow through them

questions.explanation: Transistors are called solid state because electric current moves through a solid piece of semiconductor material, unlike vacuum tubes where it crossed an empty space inside a glass tube. Option D is wrong because electricity does flow through transistors, and inductors and capacitors (B, C) are different electronic parts.

questions.question: The computers manufactured under the second generation of computers includes the following except
questions.explanation: Whirlwind was built in the early 1950s with vacuum tubes, so it is a first-generation computer. The IBM 7030, NCR 315, UNIVAC 1107 and Honeywell 700 series were transistor-based, second-generation machines.

questions.question: A temporary storage area attached to the CPU for I/O operation is a
questions.explanation: A buffer is a temporary storage area that holds data while it moves between the CPU or memory and a slower input/output device. Option D, a register, is a tiny storage location inside the CPU used for current processing, not for I/O. Option C, a bus, is a pathway that carries data rather than storing it.

questions.question: The part of the computer that interprets instructions from the software is known as the
questions.explanation: The processor (CPU) fetches, interprets and carries out the instructions given by software. Option A, memory, only holds instructions and data, and options C, D and E store data or move it in and out of the computer.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an input device?
questions.explanation: A monitor is an output device because it displays results from the computer. Keyboard, mouse, scanner and microphone (options A, B, D and E) all send data into the computer, so they are input devices.

questions.question: The main function of the ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit) is to
questions.explanation: The ALU carries out arithmetic operations such as addition and subtraction, and logical operations and comparisons such as greater than or equal to. Option C, interpreting instructions, and option E, controlling the flow of data, are jobs of the control unit. Option B, storing data, is the job of memory.

questions.question: The memory used to store instructions and data that are being actively used is called
questions.explanation: RAM is the main working memory: it holds the operating system, programs and data currently in use so the processor can reach them quickly. Option A, ROM, holds fixed start-up instructions that do not change. Options B, D and E are secondary storage, which keeps data long-term but is far too slow to serve as working memory.

questions.question: A video card is responsible for
questions.explanation: A video (graphics) card processes image data and sends it to the monitor so it can be displayed on the screen. Option D, playing sound, is the job of a sound card. Option E, connecting to the internet, is done by a network card or modem.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an input device?
questions.explanation: A mouse is an input device because it sends pointing and clicking commands into the computer. Printers, monitors, speakers and headphones (options A, B, D and E) are output devices.

questions.question: Which of the following is considered a hardware component?
questions.explanation: The processor is a physical part you can touch, so it is hardware. Windows and Linux (options A and B) are operating systems, and Excel and Photoshop (options D and E) are application software.

questions.question: Which of the following storage devices has the fastest access speed?
questions.explanation: RAM is electronic memory connected closely to the CPU, so it is much faster to access than any storage device. Options A, B, C and E, hard disks, flash drives and optical discs, are secondary storage and are far slower.

questions.question: A computer's "boot" process involves
questions.explanation: Booting is the start-up process where the computer runs its start-up program and loads the operating system into memory. Option E, rebooting, means restarting the computer, which simply repeats the boot process. Options B and C, opening applications and powering off, are not booting.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about computer memory?

options.c: RAM is used to store long-term data
options.e: RAM and ROM are both volatile

questions.explanation: ROM is non-volatile, so its contents stay even when the power is off. Options A, B and E have it backwards: RAM is volatile and ROM is non-volatile. Option C is wrong because RAM holds data only temporarily, not long-term.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of secondary memory?
questions.explanation: A hard disk is secondary memory, so it stores data permanently outside the main memory. Options A, B and D, cache, RAM and ROM, are primary memory, and option E, the processor, is not memory at all.

questions.question: Which of the following is a non-volatile memory?
questions.explanation: ROM and hard disks are both non-volatile, so they keep their data when power is switched off, which makes option E correct. Options A and B, RAM and cache, are volatile and lose their contents without power. Choosing only C or D leaves out the other correct answer.

questions.question: Which of the following devices uses a laser to read and write data?
questions.explanation: An optical drive uses a laser beam to read and write data on discs like CDs and DVDs. Options A, C and E, hard disks, floppy disks and magnetic tape, store data magnetically. Option D, a USB drive, uses flash memory chips.

questions.question: The two major types of computer chips are
questions.explanation: The two main kinds of chips in a computer are microprocessor chips, which do the processing, and memory chips, which hold data for the processor. That makes option D, both B and C, correct. Option A, external memory, means storage devices such as disks, not a type of chip.

questions.question: The brain of any computer system is
questions.explanation: The CPU is called the brain of the computer because it processes instructions and controls the other parts. Options A and D, the ALU and the control unit, are only parts of the CPU. Option B, memory, stores data but does not process it.

questions.question: Storage capacity of magnetic disk depends on
questions.explanation: A magnetic disk's capacity depends on how many tracks fit on each inch of surface, how many bits fit on each inch of track, and how many disks or surfaces are in the pack. Since all three affect capacity, option D is correct.

questions.question: The two kinds of main memory are:
questions.explanation: Main (primary) memory is made up of RAM and ROM. Option A mixes main memory with secondary storage, which is not main memory. Option B describes ways of accessing data, not kinds of memory.

questions.question: CD-ROM is a
questions.explanation: A CD-ROM is an optical storage medium: data is stored as pits and lands that are read by a laser. Option A, semiconductor memory, means chips like RAM, and option C, magnetic memory, means disks and tapes. Option B, a memory register, is inside the CPU, so none of the listed options fit.

questions.question: The ALU of a computer responds to the commands coming from
questions.explanation: The control unit (control section) sends signals that tell the ALU which operation to perform and when. Options A, C and D are kinds of memory that supply or hold data, but they do not issue commands.

questions.question: To produce high quality graphics (hardcopy) in color, you would want to use a/n
questions.explanation: A plotter draws with pens or ink on large paper and is known for producing high-quality colour graphics and drawings. Option A, an RGB monitor, gives a display on screen, not a hardcopy. Options C and D are printers, which are usually less suited to large precise drawings.

questions.question: A dumb terminal has
questions.explanation: A dumb terminal is just a keyboard and screen connected to a central computer, which does all the processing. Options A, B and C describe a computer with its own processing power and memory, which a dumb terminal does not have.

questions.question: The output quality of a printer is measured by
questions.explanation: Printer output quality, or resolution, is measured in dots per inch (dpi): the more dots per inch, the sharper the print. Option C, dots printed per unit time, measures speed, not quality. Option A is not the standard unit.

questions.question: Which of the following storage devices can store maximum amount of data?
questions.explanation: Of the options listed, a hard disk holds the most data, typically far more than floppy disks, CDs or magneto-optical disks. Option A, a floppy disk, holds only about 1.44 MB. Option C, a CD, holds about 700 MB.

questions.question: A physical connection between the microprocessor memory and other parts of the microcomputer is known as
questions.explanation: A bus is a set of wires that physically links the microprocessor to memory and the other parts of the computer, and the address bus is the bus that carries memory addresses between them. Options A and C, path and route, are everyday words rather than names of computer parts. Since those two are wrong, option D, all of the above, is wrong too.

questions.question: High density double sided floppy disks could store ____ of data
questions.explanation: A standard 3.5-inch high-density double-sided floppy disk holds 1.44 MB. Options B and C use gigabytes, which is about a thousand times too large. Option A, 1.40 MB, is close but is not the standard figure.

questions.question: A high quality CAD system uses the following for printing drawing and graphs
questions.explanation: CAD systems use digital plotters because they draw precise, high-quality lines for engineering drawings and graphs. Options A and C, dot matrix and line printers, give lower-quality output that is not suitable for detailed drawings.

questions.question: In most of the IBM PCs, the CPU, the device drivers, memory, expansion slots and active components are mounted on a single board. What is the name of the board?
questions.explanation: The motherboard is the main circuit board, holding the CPU, memory, expansion slots and other key components. Option B, a daughterboard, is a smaller board that plugs into the motherboard. Option C, a breadboard, is used for testing circuits, and option D is not a real term.

questions.question: Magnetic disks are the most popular medium for
questions.explanation: Magnetic disks are the most popular medium for direct (random) access, because the read/write head can jump straight to any track and sector. Option B, sequential access, is linked mainly with magnetic tape, where data must be read in order. A disk can also be read in sequence, but direct access is what makes it popular.

questions.question: Which of the following produces the best quality graphics reproduction?
questions.explanation: A plotter gives the best quality reproduction of graphics such as drawings and charts, because it draws precise continuous lines. Options A and B, laser and inkjet printers, are good for general printing, and option D, a dot matrix printer, gives the lowest quality.

questions.question: Before a disk drive can access any sector record, a computer program has to provide the record's disk address. What information does this address specify?
questions.explanation: To find a record on a disk, the drive needs the surface (or head) number, the track number and the sector number. Since all three make up the disk address, option D is correct.

questions.question: What is the responsibility of the logical unit in the CPU of a computer?
questions.explanation: The logic part of the ALU compares values, checking whether one is greater than, less than or equal to another. Option D, doing maths, is the arithmetic unit's job, and option C, controlling the flow of information, is the control unit's job.

questions.question: The terminal device that functions as a cash register, computer terminal, and OCR reader is the:
questions.explanation: A point-of-sale (POS) terminal works as a cash register, a computer terminal and often a reader for codes or characters at shop checkouts. Option A, a data collection terminal, only gathers data. Option B is not a standard device.

questions.question: A set of flip flops integrated together is called
questions.explanation: A register is a group of flip-flops connected together, each storing one bit, so the whole set holds a binary word. A counter (option A) is also built from flip-flops, but it is a special register made for counting. Option B, an adder, is built from logic gates.

questions.question: Which is used for manufacturing chips?
questions.explanation: Computer chips are made from semiconductor materials, mainly silicon. Options A and B, the bus and control unit, are computer parts, not manufacturing materials, so option D is also wrong.

questions.question: A register organized to allow to move left or right operations is called a
questions.explanation: A shift register can move its stored bits to the left or right, one position at a time. Option A, a counter, counts pulses, and option C, an adder, adds numbers. Option B, a loader, is a program that loads other programs, not a register.

questions.question: Which is considered a direct entry input device?
questions.explanation: Direct-entry input devices capture data directly into the computer without typing it first. Optical scanners, mice, digitizers and light pens all do this, so option D is correct.

questions.question: A computer consists of
questions.explanation: A computer has a CPU for processing, memory for storage, and input and output units for communicating with users. Since all of these are parts of a computer, option D is correct.

questions.question: What type of control pins are needed in a microprocessor to regulate traffic on the bus, in order to prevent two devices from trying to use it at the same time?
questions.explanation: Bus arbitration control signals decide which device may use the bus at a given moment, so two devices do not use it at the same time. Option B, interrupts, signal the CPU to pause for an event. Option D, status signals, report the processor's state.

questions.question: Where as a computer mouse moves over the table surface, the trackball is
questions.explanation: A trackball stays in one place, and you roll the ball with your fingers or thumb to move the pointer. This differs from a mouse, which you move across the desk. Options B, C and D wrongly suggest the trackball itself is moved.

questions.question: Which of the following is used as a primary storage device?
questions.explanation: Magnetic drums were used as the main (primary) memory in early first-generation computers. Options B and C, hard disks and floppies, are secondary storage devices, so option D is also wrong.

questions.question: What are the three decisions making operations performed by the ALU of a computer?
questions.explanation: The ALU's three basic comparisons are greater than, less than and equal to. Since all three are listed, option D is correct.

questions.question: The difference between memory and storage is that memory is ____ and storage is ____
questions.explanation: Memory such as RAM holds data temporarily while it is being used, while storage such as a hard disk keeps data permanently. Option B reverses this. Option C is wrong because memory is faster than storage, not slower.

questions.question: Which of the following memory medium is not used as main memory system?
questions.explanation: Magnetic tape can only be read sequentially and is far too slow for main memory, so it is used only for backup storage. Options A and B, magnetic core and semiconductor memory, have both been used as main memory. Option D wrongly includes semiconductors.

questions.question: The storage subsystem in a microcomputer consists mainly of ____ or ____ media with varying capacities
questions.explanation: A microcomputer's storage devices are mostly magnetic (hard and floppy disks) or optical (CDs and DVDs), with different capacities. Options A, C and D include memory or video, which are not storage media.

questions.question: Which of the following is not input unit device?
questions.explanation: A plotter is an output device that draws graphics on paper. A scanner, a camera and a digitizer (options A, B and D) all capture data and send it into the computer, so they are input devices.

questions.question: The brain of any computer system is
questions.explanation: The Central Processing Unit (CPU) is called the brain of the computer because it carries out instructions and directs all the other units. Options A and B, the control unit and ALU, are only parts of the CPU, and option D, storage, only holds data.

questions.question: The BIOS is the abbreviation of ____.
questions.explanation: BIOS stands for Basic Input Output System, the firmware that starts the computer and tests its hardware when it is switched on. Options B, C and D change one word and are not real expansions.

questions.question: Which printer is very commonly used for desktop publishing?
questions.explanation: Laser printers produce sharp, high-quality text and graphics quickly, which is exactly what desktop publishing needs. Option B, the inkjet, is common at home but is slower and less crisp for professional page layouts. Options C and D are older impact printers with poor graphics quality.

questions.question: Floppy disks are typically ____ inches in diameter
questions.explanation: Floppy disks were made in several sizes over the years: 8 inch disks came first, then 5.25 inch, and finally the small 3 to 3.5 inch disks. Since all of the listed sizes existed, option D is correct rather than any single size.

questions.question: In a computer, a ____ is capable of storing a single binary bit.
questions.explanation: A flip flop is a basic electronic circuit with two stable states, so it can hold exactly one binary bit (0 or 1). Option C, a register, is made up of a group of flip flops and stores several bits, not just one. Options A and D are ordinary electrical components, not bit-storage circuits.

questions.question: What does DMA stand for?
questions.explanation: DMA means Direct Memory Access, a method that lets devices such as disk controllers move data to and from main memory without the CPU handling every byte. The other options are made-up expansions that only sound similar.

questions.question: What is the name of the display feature that highlights an area of the screen which requires operator attention?
questions.explanation: Reverse video swaps the text and background colours of part of the screen, for example white on black instead of black on white, to make that area stand out for the operator. Option D, the cursor, only marks the current typing position, and option A, a pixel, is just a single dot on the screen.

questions.question: Registers which are partially visible to users and used to hold conditional codes (bits set by the CPU hardware as the result of operations), are known as
questions.explanation: Flags (condition code bits) are set by the CPU hardware after an operation to record results such as zero, carry or overflow, and users can only partly see them. Option D, general purpose registers, hold ordinary data, and option A, the PC, holds the address of the next instruction.

questions.question: The central processing unit (CPU) consists of

options.b: Control unit, primary storage, and secondary storage
options.c: Control unit, arithmetic-logic unit and primary storage
options.d: Control unit, processing, and primary storage

questions.explanation: In the traditional view, the CPU is made up of the control unit, the arithmetic-logic unit and primary storage (main memory). Option B wrongly includes secondary storage, which sits outside the CPU, and options A and D mix up general functions with actual units.

questions.question: Which is a semi conductor memory?
questions.explanation: Both dynamic RAM and static RAM are built from semiconductor chips, so option D is correct. Option C, bubble memory, stores data magnetically in tiny magnetic domains, so it is not a semiconductor memory.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a valid size of a Floppy Disk?
questions.explanation: Floppy disks were made in 8 inch, 5 1/4 inch and 3 1/2 inch sizes, but never 5 1/2 inch, so option D is the invalid size. Options A, B and C were all real, widely used formats.

questions.question: Which unit converts computer data into human readable form?
questions.explanation: The output unit takes processed results from memory and converts the binary codes into a form people can read or hear, such as text on a screen or a printout. Option A, the input unit, does the opposite job, and options C and D are parts of the CPU.

questions.question: The full form of ALU is
questions.explanation: ALU stands for Arithmetic Logic Unit, the part of the CPU that performs calculations and comparisons. The other expansions are made up and do not name any CPU component.

questions.question: A paper printout of a document is known as
questions.explanation: A hardcopy is output printed on paper that you can hold, carry and keep. Option A, a softcopy, is output shown on a screen or stored electronically, and option C, screen output, is just another kind of softcopy, so option D cannot be right.

questions.question: Which part of the computer is used for calculating and comparing?
questions.explanation: The ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit) carries out arithmetic such as addition and subtraction and comparisons such as greater than or equal to. Option B, the control unit, directs operations but does not calculate, and options A and D are storage and communication devices.

questions.question: A system is

options.a: an integration of different units so as to achieve an objective

questions.explanation: A system is a set of different parts working together to achieve a common objective. Options B, C and D each name only some units of a computer rather than defining what a system is.

questions.question: EEPROM stands for

options.a: Electrically Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory
options.b: Easily Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory
options.c: Electronic Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory

questions.explanation: EEPROM stands for Electrically Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory, a ROM chip that can be erased and rewritten with electrical signals. Options B and C use the wrong words, Easily and Electronic, in place of Electrically.

questions.question: Which of the following memories allows simultaneous read and write operations?
questions.explanation: RAM is read-write memory, so data can be both written to it and read from it during normal operation. ROM and EPROM (options A and C) can only be read during normal use; EPROM needs special equipment to erase and reprogram it.

questions.question: EPROM can be used for

options.c: Erasing and reconstructing the contents of ROM

questions.explanation: EPROM (Erasable Programmable ROM) can be erased, usually with ultraviolet light, and then reprogrammed with new contents. Options A and B each describe only half of what it does, and option D, duplicating ROM, is not its purpose.

questions.question: A term associated with the comparison of processing speeds of different computer system is:
questions.explanation: MIPS (Millions of Instructions Per Second) is a common measure used to compare how fast different computers process instructions. Option D, CPS (characters per second), measures printer speed, and options A and B are not computer speed measures.

questions.question: Web cam is an
questions.explanation: A webcam captures pictures and video and sends them into the computer, so it is an input device. Option D does not fit because a webcam does not display or play anything back to the user.

questions.question: Access time is
questions.explanation: Disk access time is the seek time (moving the head to the right track) plus the latency time (waiting for the right sector to rotate under the head). Options B and D give only one part, and option C wrongly subtracts them.

questions.question: Which device can understand difference between data & programs?
questions.explanation: The microprocessor fetches and decodes what is in memory, so it is the device that treats some contents as instructions to execute and others as data to work on. Memory (option C) simply holds both without telling them apart, and input and output devices (A and B) only move information in and out.

questions.question: Which of the following is a read only memory storage device?
questions.explanation: A CD-ROM (Compact Disc Read Only Memory) is pressed at manufacture, and users can read it but cannot write to it. Floppy disks and hard disks (A and C) can be both read and written.

questions.question: Primary memory stores
questions.explanation: Primary memory holds the programs being run, the data they are working on and the intermediate and final results. Since it stores all three, option D is correct rather than any single option.

questions.question: The instructions for starting the computer are housed on
questions.explanation: The startup (bootstrap) instructions are stored on a read only memory chip, so they stay in place even when the power is off. Option A, RAM, loses its contents when the computer is switched off, and option B, a CD-ROM, is not used to start a computer normally.

questions.question: The secondary storage devices can only store data but they cannot perform
questions.explanation: Secondary storage devices only hold data; arithmetic, logic and fetching instructions are all done by the CPU. Because they cannot perform any of operations A, B or C, option D is correct.

questions.question: Which of the following is not true for a magnetic disk?

options.a: It is expensive relative to magnetic tape
options.b: It provides only sequential access to stored data
options.c: Users can easily update records by writing over the old data

questions.explanation: Magnetic disks allow direct (random) access, so the read/write head can jump straight to any record, which makes option B untrue. Options A and C are true: disks cost more than tape, and records can be updated by writing over the old data.

questions.question: A disadvantage of the laser printer is

options.a: It is quieter than an impact printer
options.c: The output is of a lower quality

questions.explanation: None of the statements is a real disadvantage. Option A, being quieter than an impact printer, is an advantage, and laser printers are fast with high-quality output, so options B and C are false.

questions.question: Which access method is used to access cassette tape?
questions.explanation: A cassette tape stores data one item after another along its length, so it is read sequentially, from the start until the needed data is reached. Option A, direct access, is how disks work.

questions.question: Which unit holds data temporarily?
questions.explanation: Primary memory (RAM) holds data and programs temporarily while they are being used, and its contents are lost when the power goes off. Option B, secondary storage, keeps data permanently, while input and output units (A and C) move data rather than hold it.

questions.question: Reading data is performed in magnetic disk by
questions.explanation: Data on a magnetic disk is read and written by read/write heads that move over the spinning surface. Tracks and sectors (B and C) are the areas where data is stored, not the parts that read it.

questions.question: A hard copy would be prepared on a
questions.explanation: A hard copy is any printed output on paper, and line printers, dot matrix printers and typewriter terminals all produce printed output. Since options A, B and C all work, option D is correct.

questions.question: To locate a data item in storage is called
questions.explanation: To fetch means to locate a data item or instruction in storage and bring it out so it can be used. Option A, a field, is a single unit of data inside a record, and option C, a database, is an organised collection of data. Option B, feed, refers to supplying input such as paper or cards into a machine, not finding data in storage.

questions.question: Hard disk is coated in both sides with
questions.explanation: Hard disk platters are coated with a magnetic metal oxide layer, and data is stored by magnetising tiny spots on this surface. Option B, an optical coating, is used on CDs and DVDs, and option C, carbon, does not store data magnetically.

questions.question: An input /output device at which data enters or leaves a computer system is
questions.explanation: A terminal is a point where data can both enter and leave a computer system, usually a keyboard with a display. Options A, C and D each handle only input (keyboard) or only output (printer and plotter).

questions.question: A name or number used to identify a storage location is called
questions.explanation: An address is the unique name or number that identifies a storage location in memory. A byte (option A) is a unit of data, and a record (option B) is a group of related fields.

questions.question: The contents of information are stored in
questions.explanation: The memory data register holds the actual data being read from or written to memory. Option B, the memory address register, holds only the address of the location, not its contents, and options C and D are not standard register names.

questions.question: Main storage is also called
questions.explanation: Main storage is the computer's primary memory, so it is also simply called memory. The accumulator and other registers (A and C) are small storage areas inside the CPU, and the control unit (B) directs operations rather than storing data.

questions.question: Which of the following are (is) considered to be video component?
questions.explanation: Resolution (number of pixels), colour depth (number of colours) and refresh rate (how often the screen redraws) all describe video display quality. Since options A, B and C are all video components, option D is correct.

questions.question: Memory unit is one part of
questions.explanation: In the classic model of a computer, the memory unit is treated as part of the central processing unit, together with the control unit and the ALU. Options A and C are peripheral devices, and the control unit (B) is a separate part that directs operations.

questions.question: Which of the following is a secondary memory device?
questions.explanation: A disk, such as a hard disk, stores data permanently and is a secondary memory device. Option A, the keyboard, is an input device, and option C, the ALU, is part of the CPU.

questions.question: The memory which is programmed at the time it is manufactured
questions.explanation: ROM is programmed when the chip is manufactured, and its contents cannot be changed by users. Option C, PROM, is supplied blank and programmed later by the user, and option D, EPROM, can be erased and reprogrammed, while RAM (option B) is not programmed at all.

questions.question: One of the popular mass storage device is CD ROM. What does CD ROM stand for?
questions.explanation: CD-ROM stands for Compact Disk Read Only Memory, an optical disc that users can read but not write. Options A, B and C use the wrong words, such as Compactable or Data, in place of Compact Disk.

questions.question: Which of the following memories must be refreshed many times per second?
questions.explanation: Dynamic RAM stores each bit as a tiny charge in a capacitor that leaks away, so it must be refreshed many times every second. Option A, static RAM, uses flip flops that hold data without refreshing, and ROM and EPROM (C and D) keep their contents without power.

questions.question: Serial access memories are useful in applications where

options.c: Each stored word is processed differently
options.d: Data naturally needs to flow in and out in serial form

questions.explanation: Serial access memory reads and writes data in order, one item after another, so it suits applications where data naturally flows in and out in sequence. Option B is wrong because serial access is slow for jumping to a particular item.

questions.question: Memory is made up of
questions.explanation: Memory is made up of a very large number of cells, each able to store a bit or a group of bits and each with its own address. Options A and B describe wiring and circuitry in general, not the organised structure of memory.

questions.question: Which of the printers used in conjunction with computers uses dry ink powder?
questions.explanation: Laser printers use toner, a dry ink powder that is fused onto the paper with heat. Daisy wheel and line printers (A and B) strike an inked ribbon, and thermal printers (D) use heat-sensitive paper.

questions.question: Which term is used to describe RAM?
questions.explanation: Dynamic RAM, static RAM and video RAM are all types of random access memory. Since options A, B and C all describe RAM, option D is correct.

questions.question: Which of the following storage device can store the largest amount of data?
questions.explanation: Hard disks offer the largest storage capacities of the devices listed, often several terabytes. Flash disks, Blu-ray discs and DVDs (B, C and D) usually hold much less, with a DVD storing only a few gigabytes.

questions.question: As compared to diskettes, the hard disks are
questions.explanation: Hard disks cost more than diskettes but store much more and work much faster. Option B is wrong because diskettes are the portable ones, option C because hard disks use rigid platters, and option D because hard disks are accessed faster.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most quickly accessible storage?
questions.explanation: Registers are tiny storage locations inside the CPU itself, so they are the fastest storage to access. RAM (option A) is fast but sits outside the processor, and disks and pen drives (C and D) are much slower.

questions.question: Can you tell what passes into and out from the computer via its ports?
questions.explanation: Ports are connection points through which data passes into and out of the computer. Bytes, graphics and pictures (B, C and D) are all just particular forms of data, so data is the most complete answer.

questions.question: An output device that uses words or messages recorded on a magnetic medium to produce audio response is
questions.explanation: A voice response unit plays back stored words or messages to produce spoken output. Option C, voice recognition, is an input technology that understands speech, and option A, magnetic tape, is a storage medium.

questions.question: Which of the items below are considered removable storage media?
questions.explanation: Removable hard disk cartridges, magneto-optical disks and flexible disk cartridges can all be taken out of the computer and carried elsewhere. Since options A, B and C are all removable media, option D is correct.

questions.question: Which of the following is not purely output device?
questions.explanation: A screen can also act as an input device when it is a touch screen, so it is not purely an output device. Printers, speakers and plotters (B, C and D) only produce output.

questions.question: The control unit of a microprocessor
questions.explanation: The control unit directs and coordinates the other parts of the computer; it does not store data, accept input or perform calculations itself. Option C describes the ALU, option A the memory, and option B the input unit.

questions.question: Which of the following is internal memory?
questions.explanation: RAM is internal (primary) memory connected directly to the processor. Disks, pen drives and CDs (A, B and D) are secondary or external storage devices.

questions.question: Floppy disks which are made from flexible plastic material are also called?
questions.explanation: Floppy disks made of flexible plastic are also called diskettes. Option A, hard disks, use rigid platters, and option B, high-density, describes a storage capacity, not the disk type.

questions.question: The magnetic storage chip used to provide non-volatile direct access storage of data and that have no moving parts are known as
questions.explanation: Magnetic bubble memory stores data in tiny magnetised areas on a chip, giving non-volatile storage with no moving parts. Magnetic tape and magnetic disk (B and C) rely on moving parts, and core memory (A) is made of tiny magnetic rings rather than a chip.

questions.question: Plotter accuracy is measured in terms of repeatability and
questions.explanation: Plotter accuracy depends on repeatability (returning to the same point) and resolution (the smallest movement the pen can make). Buffer size (option A) affects speed rather than accuracy, and options C and D are not accuracy measures.

questions.question: Which of the following processors use RISC technology?
questions.explanation: The PowerPC processor uses RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computing) technology. The 486DX and 486SX (options A and C) are Intel x86 chips that use a CISC design.

questions.question: Which of the following terms is the most closely related to main memory?
questions.explanation: Main memory (RAM) holds the programs and data in current use only temporarily, and its contents are lost when power goes off. Non-volatile and permanent (A, B) describe ROM or secondary storage, and the control unit (C) is part of the CPU, not memory.

questions.question: A group of magnetic tapes, videos or terminals usually under the control of one master is
questions.explanation: A cluster is a group of devices, such as tape drives or terminals, that share a single controller acting as the master. Cylinder, surface and track (A, B, C) are terms describing how data is laid out on a disk.

questions.question: What type of memory is not directly addressable by the CPU and requires special software called EMS (expanded memory specification)?
questions.explanation: Expanded memory was extra memory beyond the old DOS limit that the CPU could not address directly; it was reached by swapping pages in and out using the EMS standard. Extended memory (A) is addressed directly by the CPU, while base and conventional memory (C, D) are the normal first 640 KB.

questions.question: Which unit holds data permanently?
questions.explanation: Secondary storage, such as a hard disk, keeps data permanently even after the computer is switched off. Primary memory (D) mainly holds data temporarily, and the input and output units (A, C) move data in and out rather than store it.

questions.question: Before a disk can be used to store data. It must be
questions.explanation: Formatting prepares a new disk by setting up its tracks, sectors and file system so data can be stored on it. Reformatting (B) is only needed later to wipe or redo a disk, and addressing (C) is not the preparation step.

questions.question: Computer system comprises of major units

options.a: input unit, output unit, control unit
options.b: input unit, output unit, control unit and storage
options.c: input unit, output unit, central processing unit and storage unit

questions.explanation: A computer system is made up of input units, output units, the central processing unit and storage units. Option A leaves out storage and lists only the control unit instead of the whole CPU, while B and D also miss the CPU or part of it.

questions.question: Which of the following file organization is most efficient for a file with a high degree of file activity?
questions.explanation: When a large share of records is processed in each run (high file activity), sequential organization is most efficient because the file is simply read straight through. Indexed methods like ISAM, VSAM and B-tree (B, C, D) are better when only a few records are needed at a time.

questions.question: Magnetic tape can serve as
questions.explanation: Magnetic tape can store data for backup (secondary storage), and data can be written to it as output or read from it as input. Choosing only A ignores that tape also works as an input and output medium, so D is the best answer.

questions.question: MICR stands for
questions.explanation: MICR stands for Magnetic Ink Character Reader (also called Magnetic Ink Character Recognition), the technology banks use to read the magnetic-ink numbers on cheques. 'Code Reader' and 'Cases Reader' (B, C) are not the correct expansion.

questions.question: Which technology is used in Compact disks?
questions.explanation: Compact discs are optical media: a laser reads the tiny pits and lands on the disc surface. Mechanical, electrical and electromagnetic methods (A, B, C) describe other storage types, such as magnetic disks, not CDs.

questions.question: Different components of the motherboard of a PC unit are linked together by sets of parallel electrical conducting lines. What are these lines called?
questions.explanation: Buses are sets of parallel conducting lines that carry data, addresses and control signals between components on the motherboard. Conductors and connectors (A, C) are general terms, and 'consecutives' (D) is not a computer term.

questions.question: Which of the following is a storage device?
questions.explanation: Tape, hard disks and floppy disks are all storage media that keep data and programs for later use. Since A, B and C are each storage devices, D is correct.

questions.question: The metal disks, which are permanently housed in, sealed and contamination free containers are called
questions.explanation: Winchester disks are hard disks whose rigid metal platters and read/write heads are sealed in a contamination-free housing. Compact discs (A) are optical plastic discs, and floppy and flexible disks (B, D) are removable plastic disks that are not sealed.

questions.question: CD-ROM stands for
questions.explanation: CD-ROM stands for Compact Disk Read Only Memory, an optical disc whose data can be read but not changed. 'Compactable' and 'Compact Data' (A, B, C) are not the correct words in the expansion.

questions.question: Which unit converts user data into machine readable form?
questions.explanation: The input unit accepts data from the user and converts it into binary codes the computer can read. The output unit (B) does the reverse, and the ALU and control unit (C, D) process and coordinate data that is already inside.

questions.question: Which unit is known as nerve center of computer?
questions.explanation: The control unit is called the nerve centre because it directs and coordinates all the other parts of the computer, just as nerves carry signals around the body. The ALU (A) only performs calculations and comparisons, and memory and registers (C, D) only hold data.

questions.question: Through which device the main components of the computer communicate with each other?
questions.explanation: The system bus is the set of electrical pathways that lets the CPU, memory and input/output devices communicate. The keyboard and monitor (A, C) are input and output devices, and memory (D) is one of the parts connected by the bus.

questions.question: What type of device is computer keyboard?
questions.explanation: A keyboard is an input device: you use it to type data and commands into the computer. It does not display results (B) or store data (A, C).

questions.question: The full form of EEPROM is

options.a: Electrically Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory
options.b: Easily Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory
options.c: Electronic Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory

questions.explanation: EEPROM stands for Electrically Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory, which can be erased and reprogrammed electrically. 'Easily' and 'Electronic' (B, C) are wrong words in the expansion.

questions.question: The ALU of a computer normally contains a number of high speed storage element called
questions.explanation: Registers are small, very fast storage locations inside the CPU that hold the data the ALU is working on. Semiconductor memory, hard disks and magnetic disks (A, C, D) are main memory or secondary storage outside the ALU.

questions.question: A kind of scanner MICR is the short form of
questions.explanation: MICR stands for Magnetic Ink Character Reader (also called Recognition), a scanner-type device banks use to read magnetic-ink characters on cheques. 'Code Reader' and 'Cases Reader' (B, C) are not the correct expansion.

questions.question: Which of the following disk is fixed disk?
questions.explanation: A hard disk is a fixed disk: its rigid platters are sealed inside the drive and normally stay in the computer. Flash disks, Blu-ray discs and DVDs (B, C, D) are removable media.

questions.question: An online backing storage system capable of storing larger quantities of data is
questions.explanation: Mass storage refers to online backing storage systems designed to hold very large quantities of data. Cache memory (D) is a tiny, very fast store inside or near the CPU, so it holds far less data, and the CPU and main memory (A, B) are not backing storage at all.

questions.question: A kind of serial dot-matrix printer that forms characters with electrically charged ink droplets sprayed onto the paper is called
questions.explanation: An ink-jet printer forms characters from tiny charged droplets of ink sprayed onto the paper, printing one character position at a time. Laser printers (A) use toner and a drum, and drum and chain printers (C, D) are impact line printers.

questions.question: Which of the following does not affect the resolution of a video display image?

options.c: Vertical and horizontal lines of resolution

questions.explanation: Resolution depends on how many lines and pixels the display can produce, which is set by bandwidth, raster scan rate and the number of vertical and horizontal lines. Screen size (D) only changes how big the picture is, not how many pixels it has, so A, B and C do affect resolution.

questions.question: The number of records contained within a block of data on magnetic tape is defined by the
